subtype_info: pulmonary tuberculosis in a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis treated with contezolid
title: Tuberculosis patients with special clinical conditions treated with contezolid: three case reports and a literature review
case_text:
A 49 years-old woman was diagnosed with alcoholic cirrhosis 3 years ago and denied family or genetic history of chronic diseases, cancer, or psychiatric disorders. One year ago, the patient presented with a cough, white phlegm, night sweats, fatigue, and an occasional afternoon fever. She was admitted to a local hospital, and sputum smear results showed positive for acid-fast bacilli (2+). Due to the patient's alcoholic cirrhosis, she was given isoniazid, ethambutol, rifapentine, and levofloxacin for anti-TB treatment for half a year. The patient felt that her health had improved and stopped taking the drug on her own. In December 2021, due to the recurrence of cough and sputum, she went to the local hospital. After 1 month of oral anti-TB drugs, she stopped taking anti-TB drugs again due to nausea and poor appetite. One week before admission, a cough and sputum appeared, with blood in the sputum, and the results of the sputum examination in the outpatient department of our hospital were positive for acid-fast bacilli (3+). Symptomatic hemostasis treatment was given, and hemoptysis was stopped. She was admitted to the hospital on 14 September 2022.
On laboratory findings, her WBC was 5.05 x 109/L with a neutrophil ratio of 70.5%, HGB was 70 g/L, and PLT was 87 x 109/L. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) was 10 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was 17 U/L, total bilirubin (TB) was 21.8 mumol/L, direct bilirubin (DB) was 7.6 mumol/L, and albumin (ALB) was 29 g/L. Smear results of sputum showed positive for acid-fast bacilli (4+). The Xpert results showed that the positive DNA content of TB bacteria was medium and there was no mutational resistance. Culture results of sputum showed M. tuberculosis complex positive. The drug sensitivity test for sputum showed that the patient was resistant to isoniazid, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin and sensitive to rifampin. The results of drug resistance gene detection in M. tuberculosis showed mutations in the isoniazid resistance gene, ethambutol resistance gene, and quinolone resistance gene. CT showed that both lungs have multiple patches and cavities (Figure 3A).
Considering the patient had cirrhosis and secondary anemia, pyrazinamide and linezolid were not used. She was given amikacin (0.4 g/qd, intravenously), contezolid (200 mg/q12h, orally), and rifapentine (0.45 g/biw, orally). Meanwhile, liver protection and iron sucrose were given to treat anemia. On 26 October 2022 (day 42 after treatment), sputum smear results showed negative for acid-fast bacilli. After 60 days of treatment, the blood routine showed WBC was 3.19 x 109/L, HGB was 110 g/L, and PLT was 83 x 109/L. The patient felt that her cough and sputum symptoms had significantly improved, that her body weight increased by 4 kg, and that she had no limb numbness. CT showed that both lung consolidation shadows were absorbed, and both pulmonary cavities were smaller than before (Figure 3B). On 26 November 2022 (day 73 after treatment), sputum smear results showed negative for acid-fast bacilli. The administration process is shown in Figure 2B.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: pulmonary tuberculosis in a patient with alcoholic cirrhosis treated with contezolid
